lines.text: Colours are one of the first vocabulary sets every language learner masters, yet English has a remarkably rich and nuanced colour vocabulary. The primary colours — red, blue, and yellow — combine to create secondary colours: orange (red + yellow), green (blue + yellow), and purple (red + blue). Black and white are considered achromatic — without colour — while grey sits between them. Brown, pink, and turquoise are common colours that don't fit neatly into the primary-secondary system. English distinguishes between light and dark shades: light blue versus dark blue, pale green versus deep green. Colours can be described as bright, vivid, bold, and vibrant for intensity, or muted, dull, pastel, and faded for softness. The colour spectrum follows the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet — remembered by the mnemonic 'Roy G. Biv'. Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) evoke energy and heat, while cool colours (blues, greens, purples) suggest calm and nature. Neutral colours — beige, cream, ivory, taupe — are popular in fashion and interior design. Metallic colours like gold, silver, and bronze add luxury. Cultural associations vary enormously: white symbolises purity in Western culture but mourning in some Eastern cultures; green represents nature but also envy. Mastering colour vocabulary enhances descriptions of art, fashion, nature, and everyday objects.

lines.text: British English spells it 'colour', American English uses 'color'. The same pattern applies to: grey (UK) vs gray (US), though both are widely accepted. This difference extends to 'colourful/colorful', 'favourite/favorite', etc.

lines.text: English colour symbolism: red = love/danger/anger; blue = sadness/trust/calm; green = nature/envy/eco; white = purity/peace; black = death/elegance/mystery; yellow = happiness/caution; gold = wealth/success; purple = royalty/luxury.

lines.text: English uses food names for colours: peach, plum, cherry, lemon, lime, olive, salmon, chocolate, cream, ivory, champagne, burgundy (wine), tangerine, mint. These are widely used in fashion and design contexts.

lines.text: Colours appear in countless expressions: 'red tape' (bureaucracy), 'green light' (permission), 'grey area' (ambiguous), 'blacklist' (banned), 'white lie' (harmless lie), 'golden age' (best period), 'silver tongue' (eloquence).
